¶
'''thaumaturgism''' (thâ-ma-tėr′jizm), ''n.'' Magic, as a pretended science; thaumaturgy (which is the better word).

'''thaumaturgist''' (thâ′ma-tėr-jist), ''n.'' [< ''thaumaturg-y'' + ''-ist.''] Same as ''thaumaturge.''

{{smaller block|Cagliostro, ''Thaumaturgist,'' Prophet, and Arch-Quack.
{{right|''Carlyle,'' Diamond Necklace, xvi.}}}}

'''thaumaturgus''' (thâ-ma-tėr′gus), ''n.''; pl. ''thaumaturgi'' (-jī). [ML., < Gr. θαυματουργός, wonder-working: see ''thaumaturge.''] A thaumaturge or thaumaturgist: used especially as a title of Gregory Thaumaturgus (bishop of Neocæsarea in Pontus in the third century), from the numerous and wonderful miracles ascribed to him.

{{smaller block|Nature, the great ''Thaumaturgus,'' has in the Vocal Memnon propounded an enigma of which it is beyond the scope of existing knowledge to supply more than a hypothetically correct solution.
{{right|''Edinburgh Rev.,'' CLXIV. 283.}}}}

'''thaumaturgy''' (thâ′ma-tėr-ji), ''n.'' [= F. ''thaumaturgie,'' < Gr. θαυματουργία, a working of wonders, < θαυματουργός, wonder-working: see ''thaumaturge.''] The act of performing something wonderful or marvelous; wonder-working; magic.

{{smaller block|But in those despotic countries the Police is so arbitrary! Cagliostro's ''thaumaturgy'' must be overhauled by the Empress's physician . . . is found nought.
{{right|''Carlyle,'' Cagliostro.}}
His reporters . . . are men who saw ''thaumaturgy'' in all that Jesus did.
{{right|''M. Arnold,'' Literature and Dogma, v.}}}}

'''thave,''' ''n.'' See ''theave.''

'''thaw''' (thâ), ''v.'' [Also dial. ''thow;'' < ME. ''thawen, thowen,'' < AS. ''thāwian'' = D. ''dooijen'' = OHG. ''towan, douwen, dowen'' (''dōan''), MHG. ''touwen, töuwen,'' G. ''tauen,'' thaw, digest, = Icel. ''theyja''

{{smaller block|The winter gives them [flowers] rest under ''thawless'' serenity of snow.
{{right|''Ruskin,'' in St. James's Gazette, Feb. 9, 1886. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''thawy''' (thâ′i), ''a.'' [< ''thaw'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Growing liquid; thawing; inclined to thaw.

{{smaller block|Of a warm ''thawy'' day in February, the snow is suddenly covered with myriads of snow fleas.
{{right|''The Century,'' XXV. 679.}}}}

'''the'''<sup>1</sup> (ᴛ̵ʜē, ᴛ̵ʜẹ̄, or ᴛ̵ʜē̤), ''def. art.'' [< ME. ''the,'' < AS. ''the,'' rare as an article but common as a relative, f. ''theó,'' also rare, neut. ''thæt,'' the; the usual forms being ''se,'' m., ''seó,'' f., ''thæt,'' neut., with the base ''the'' (''tha-'') appearing in all the oblique forms (gen. ''thæs,'' m., ''thǣre,'' f., ''thæs,'' neut.; dat. ''tham, thære, tham;'' acc. ''thane'' or ''thone, thā, thæt;'' instr. ''thȳ'' or ''thē, thǣre, thȳ'' or ''thē;'' pl. for all genders, nom. acc. ''thā,'' gen. ''thāra,'' dat. instr. ''thām, thǣm''); = OS. ''the'' = OFries. ''thi,'' the, = D. ''de'' = MLG. LG. ''de'' = OHG. MHG. ''der, diu, daz,'' G. ''der, die, das,'' the, that, = Icel. ''that,'' the, = Sw.

[< ''thaw'' + ''-y''1.] Growing liquid; thawing; inclined to thaw. {{smaller block|Of a warm ''thawy'' day in February, the snow is suddenly covered with myriads of snow fleas. {{right|''The Century,'' XXV. 679.}}}} '''the'''1 (ᴛ̵ʜē, ᴛ̵ʜẹ̄, or ᴛ̵ʜē̤), ''def. art.'' [< ME. ''the,'' < AS. ''the,'' rare as an article but common as a relative, f. ''theó,'' also rare, neut. ''thæt,'' the; the usual forms being ''se,'' m., ''seó,'' f., ''thæt,'' neut., with the base ''the'' (''tha-'') appearing in all the oblique forms (gen. ''thæs,'' m., ''thǣre,'' f., ''thæs,'' neut.; dat. ''tham, thære, tham;'' acc. ''thane'' or ''thone, thā, thæt;'' instr. ''thȳ'' or ''thē, thǣre, thȳ'' or ''thē;'' pl. for all genders, nom. acc. ''thā,'' gen. ''thāra,'' dat. instr. ''thām, thǣm''); = OS. ''the'' = OFries. ''thi,'' the, = D. ''de'' = MLG. LG. ''de'' = OHG. MHG. ''der, diu, daz,'' G. ''der, die, das,'' the, that, = Icel. ''that,'' the, = Sw. (cf. ''thā'', a thaw, ''theyr'', a thaw) = Sw. ''töa'' = Dan. ''tö'' (Goth. not recorded), thaw; root uncertain.] I. ''intrans.'' 1. To pass from a frozen to a liquid or semi-fluid state; melt; dissolve: said of ice or snow; also, to be freed from frost; have the contained frost dissolved by heat: said of anything frozen. {{smaller block|Dire hail which on firm land
''Thaws'' not. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 590.}}}} 2. To become so warm as to melt ice and snow; rise above a temperature of 32° Fahrenheit: said of the weather, and used impersonally.—3. To be released from any condition, physical or mental, resembling that of freezing; become supple, warm, or genial; be freed from coldness, embarrassment, formality, or reserve; unbend: often with ''out.'' {{smaller block|The bog's green harper, ''thawing'' from his sleep,
Twangs a hoarse note and tries a shortened leap. {{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Spring.}}}} {{smaller block|Arthur took a long time ''thawing'', . . . was sadly timid. {{right|''T. Hughes'', Tom Brown at Rugby, ii. 2.}}}} II. ''trans.'' 1. To reduce from a frozen to a liquid state, as ice or snow; also, to free from frost, as some frozen substance: often with ''out.''—2. To render less cold, formal, or stiff; free from embarrassment, shyness, or reserve; make chanical misdivision of ''thet other'', ''thet one'', i. e. ''that other'', ''that one'' (see ''tother'', ''tone''2). It may be noted that initial ''th'' (AS. þ or ð) is in ''the'' and all the words of this group pronounced ᴛ̵ʜ, while in all other cases it is in mod. E. always pronounced th.] 1. A word used before nouns with a specifying or particularizing effect, opposed to the indefinite or generalizing force of ''a'' or ''an'': as, ''the'' gods are careless of mankind; ''the'' sun in heaven; ''the'' day is fair; long live ''the'' king! {{smaller block|Zuych [such] wyt zet ''the'' holy gost ine herte. {{right|''Ayenbite of Inwyt'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 251.}}}} {{smaller block|In a somere seyson, whan softe was ''the'' sonne. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|Out went ''the'' taper as she hurried in. {{right|''Keats'', Eve of St. Agnes.}}}} 2. A word used before a noun to indicate a species or genus: as, the song of ''the'' nightingale: used in generalization: as, ''the'' man that hath no music in himself. {{smaller block|''The'' mellow plum doth fall, ''the'' green sticks fast. {{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 527.}}}} 3. A word used with a title, or as part of a title: as, ''the'' Duke of Wellington; ''the'' Right Honorable ''the'' Earl of Derby; ''the'' Lord Brook; ''the'' Reverend John Smith. {{smaller|Frequently, with more or less of technical accuracy, ''the'' is omitted, especially}} genial: often with ''out.'' {{smaller block|''Thaw'' this male nature to some touch of that
Which . . . drags me down . . . to mob me up with all
The soft and milky rabble of womankind. {{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, vi.}}}} {{smaller block|With a hopeless endeavor to ''thaw'' him ''out'' and return good for evil, I ventured to remark that . . . the general had, during the evening, highly entertained us by reading some of his (Mr. P.'s) poetry. {{right|''J. Jefferson'', Autobiog., xii.}}}} {{smaller|=Syn. 1. ''Dissolve, Fuse'', etc. See ''melt''1.}} '''thaw''' (thâ), ''n.'' [= Icel. ''thā'' (also ''theyr'') = Sw. Dan. ''tö'', a thaw; from the verb.] 1. The melting of ice or snow; also, the melting by heat of any substance congealed by frost. {{smaller block|Still, as ice
More harden'd after ''thaw.'' {{right|''Milton'', P. L., xii. 194.}}}} {{smaller block|If the Sun of Righteousness should arise upon him, his frozen heart shall feel a ''thaw.'' {{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim's Progress, ii.}}}} 2. Warmth of weather, such as liquefies or melts anything congealed. {{smaller block|She told me . . . that I was duller than a great ''thaw.'' {{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, ii. 1. 252.}}}} {{smaller block|The day after our arrival a ''thaw'' set in, which cleared away every particle of snow and ice. {{right|''B. Taylor'', Northern Travel, p. 24.}}}} 3. The state of becoming less cold, formal, or reserved.—{{smaller|'''Silver thaw''', glazed frost; the frozen surface which is occasionally produced at the beginning of a thaw, or when a fall of rain or mist occurs while the air-temperature at the earth's surface is below 32° F.}} '''thaw-drop''' (thâ′drop), ''n.'' A drop of water formed by melting snow or ice. {{smaller block|She gave me one cold parting kiss upon my forehead,}} when the distinctive title is not followed by ''of:'' as, ''Earl'' Grey, ''Viscount'' Palmerston. With the designation ''Lord'', as applied to a peer of any rank, ''the'' is generally omitted: ''the'' Marquis of Salisbury, for instance, is frequently styled ''Lord'' Salisbury. In Scotland and Ireland, ''the'' is sometimes placed before family names with somewhat of the force of a title, indicating the head of the clan or family: as, ''the'' Macnab; ''the'' O'Donoghue. {{smaller block|At last ''the'' Duglas and ''the'' Persè [Percy] met,
Lyk to [two] captayns of myght and of mayne. {{right|''The Hunting of the Cheviot'' (Child's Ballads, VII. 35).}}}} {{smaller block|I became acquainted with ''the'' Mulligan through a distinguished countryman of his, who, strange to say, did not know the chieftain himself. . . . The greatest offence that can be offered to him is to call him Mr. Mulligan. {{right|''Thackeray'', Mrs. Perkins's Ball.}}}} 4. Indicating the most approved, most desirable, most conspicuous, or most important of its kind: as, Newport is ''the'' watering-place of the United States: in this use emphatic, and frequently italicized. ''The'' is often placed before a person's (especially a woman's) name, to indicate admiration or notoriety (a colloquial use): as, ''the'' Elssler. {{smaller block|Joel Burns was a rich man, as well as ''the'' man of the place. {{right|''R. B. Kimball'', Was He Successful? vi.}}}} 5. Before adjectives used substantively, denoting: (''a'') An individual: as, she gazed long on the face of ''the'' dead. {{smaller block|''The'' dead
Steer'd by the dumb went upward with the flood. {{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}} (''b'') A class, or a number of individuals: as, ''the'' good die first; do not mix ''the'' new with ''the'' old. {{smaller block|Now this, . . . though it make ''the'' unskilful laugh, cannot but make ''the'' judicious grieve. like a ''thaw-drop'' from the stone porch—it was a very frosty day. {{right|''Dickens'', Bleak House, iii.}}}} '''thawless''' (thâ′les), ''a.'' [< ''thaw'' + ''-less''.] Without a thaw; not thawing: as, a ''thawless'' winter. {{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iii. 2. 29.}}}} (''c'') An abstract notion: as, ''the'' beautiful. {{smaller block|One step above ''the'' sublime makes ''the'' ridiculous. {{right|''T. Paine'', Age of Reason, ii.}}}} 6. Denoting that which is well known or famed: as, ''the'' prodigal son. {{smaller block|Like ''the'' poor cat i' the adage. {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, i. 7. 45.}} Cry, like ''the'' daughters of ''the'' horseleech, “Give!” {{right|''Tennyson'', Golden Year.}}}} 7. Used distributively to denote any one separately: as, the fare is a dollar ''the'' round trip. {{smaller block|So muche money as will byy the same [gunpowder] after xiijd ''the'' pound. {{right|''Sir H. Knevett'' (1588), quoted in H. Hall's Society in the [Elizabethan Age, App. ii.}} The country inn cannot supply anything except brandied sherry at five shillings ''the'' bottle. {{right|''Mortimer Collins'', Thoughts in my Garden, I. 85.}}}} 8. Used in place of the possessive pronoun to denote a personal belonging: as, to hang ''the'' head and weep. {{smaller block|Is there none of Pygmalion's images . . . to be had now, for putting ''the'' hand in ''the'' pocket? {{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iii. 2. 49.}} Voltaire is the prince of buffoons: . . . he shakes ''the'' sides; he points ''the'' finger; he turns up ''the'' nose; he shoots out ''the'' tongue. {{right|''Macaulay'', Addison.}}}} 9. Used to denote a particular day in relation to a given week, or to some other day of the same week. [Obsolete or colloq.] {{smaller block|I m̄ene, if God please, to be at Salisburie ''the'' wekes-daie at night before Easterdaie. {{right|''Sir J. Popham'' (1582), quoted in H. Hall's Society in the [Elizabethan Age, App. ii.}} Mrs. Proudie had died on ''the'' Tuesday, . . . and Mr. Robarts had gone over to Silverbridge on ''the'' Thursday. {{right|''Trollope'', Last Chronicle of Barset, lxviii.}}}} 10. Used before a participial infinitive, or gerund, followed by an object: the article is now omitted in this construction. {{smaller block|He alter'd much upon ''the'' hearing it. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iv. 5. 12.}}}} 11. Used before the relative ''which'': now an archaism. {{smaller block|Clerkes of holikirke that kepen Crystes tresore, ''The'' which is mannes soul to saue. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), x. 474.}}}} {{smaller block|[''The'' is generally pronounced as if a syllable (unaccented) of the following word (a proclitic), and its vowel is accordingly obscured, before a consonant, into the neutral vowel-sound of ''her'' or ''but'', very lightly sounded (quite like the French "mute ''e''"); before a vowel, often in the same manner, but more usually with the short ''i'' sound of ''pin'', only less distinct; when emphatic, as the long ''e'' of ''thee''. In poetry, before a word beginning with a vowel-sound, the vowel of ''the'' generally may slide into that of the next word, and form with it one metrical syllable; metrically the ''e'' is accordingly often cut off in printing. The same so-called elision (synalephe) often took place in Middle English, ''the'' being written with the following noun as one word: as, ''themperour'', the emperor.}} {{smaller block|''Th''' one sweetly flatters, ''th''' other feareth harm. {{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 172.}}}} {{smaller block|In Middle English manuscripts ''the'' was often written, as in Anglo-Saxon þe, with the character þ; in early print this character was represented by a form nearly like ''y'', and later printers actually used ''y'' instead, þe, erroneously printed þe as if contracted, like þt for ''that'', being printed ''ye'' or ''ye'', but always pronounced, of course, ''the''. Modern archaists often affect ''ye'' for ''the'', and many pronounce it as it looks, "yē."}} {{smaller block|And on ''ye'' Tewsday at nyght we passed by the yle of Pathemos. {{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 14.}}}} {{smaller block|We afterwards fell into a dispute with a Candiot concerning the procession of ''ye'' Holy Ghost. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, June, 1645.]}}}} '''the2''' (ᴛ̵ʜē, ᴛ̵ʜẹ̄, or ᴛ̵ʜē̤), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''the'', ''thi'', < AS. ''thē'', ''thȳ'' = OS. ''thiu'', ''diu'', weakened ''te'', ''de'' as an enclitic in ''des te'', ''des de'' = D. ''des te'' = MLG. ''deste'', ''duste'' = MHG. ''deste'', ''dest'', G. ''desto'' (cf. AS. ''thæs the'') = Dan. ''des'', ''desto'' = Sw. ''dess'', ''desto'' = Icel. ''thvī'', ''thī'' = Goth. ''thē'', instr. of ''thata'' (AS. ''thæt''): see ''that'', ''the''1.] Used to modify adjectives and adverbs in the comparative degree: {{smaller|(''a'') Correlatively, having in the first instance a relative force, = by how much, and in the second a demonstrative force, = by so much: as, ''the'' sooner ''the'' better; ''the'' more ''the'' merrier.}} {{smaller block|''The'' mightier man, ''the'' mightier is the thing That makes him honour'd, or begets him hate. {{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1004.}}}} {{smaller block|And ''the'' sooner it 's over ''the'' sooner to sleep. {{right|''Kingsley'', The Fishermen.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') Used without correlation, it signifies in any degree; in some degree: as, Are you well? ''The'' better for seeing you.}} {{smaller block|Al for loue of owre lorde, and ''the'' bet to loue the peple. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xi. 169.}}}} {{smaller block|Thou shalt not be ''the'' worse for me; there 's gold. {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., v. 1. 30.}}}} '''the3†''', ''v. i.'' See ''thee''1. '''the4†''', ''conj.'' A Middle English form of ''though''. '''the5†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''thigh''. '''Thea''' (thē′ä̤), ''n.'' [NL. (Linnæus, 1737): see ''tea''1.] A former genus of plants, now included as a section under ''Camellia'', and comprising the species yielding tea. See cuts under ''tea''1. '''T-head''' (tē′hed), ''n.'' 1. A cross-bar fastened at its middle to a chain, as a watch-chain, trace-chain, etc., for use as a fastening by passing it
